network_relevancy_priority.problem: In a server-authoritative replicated-actor model, every replicated actor must decide, on every network update, whether each connected client needs an update. That decision cost is O(actors x connections) per tick, and it lands on the same server CPU that has to finish the simulation inside its frame budget. Epic states the canonical failure case: Fortnite Battle Royale starts each match with 100 connected players and about 50,000 replicated actors, at which point the default 'each replicated Actor evaluates each connected client' strategy 'performs poorly ... and will bottleneck the server's CPU'. Riot describes the same cost from the other side: replication 'requires scanning through every variable marked as replicated every frame, then comparing it to each of the 10 clients' last known states, and then packaging any deltas'. The naive mitigations - staggered groups, lower update frequency - degrade the client experience rather than removing the cost. Relevancy + priority is the family of techniques that precompute and cache the answer instead of recomputing it per connection per tick.

implementation_variants.name: Grid/zone spatial partitioning node (Unreal Replication Graph)
implementation_variants.description: Divide the world into grid cells (battle royale / MOBA / MMO) or predefined rooms/zones (corridor shooters), add each actor to every cell it could be seen or heard from, and serve the client the persistent actor list for the cell its camera is in. Relevancy becomes a lookup instead of a per-actor per-connection test.

implementation_variants.name: Dormancy list for level-placed static actors
implementation_variants.description: Separate actors that never change on their own (trees, props) into their own list so they cost nothing per frame until they are damaged/destroyed, at which point only clients that can see them get the update. Epic uses exactly this example for Fortnite.

implementation_variants.name: Always-relevant and team-reveal lists
implementation_variants.description: Maintain small explicit lists for actors always relevant to everyone, always relevant to a specific player/team (e.g. teammates), or temporarily revealed by an ability. This keeps them out of the expensive general lists while guaranteeing no gameplay-critical actor is ever culled by mistake.

implementation_variants.name: Per-connection dirty-variable scan (the default model this replaces)
implementation_variants.description: Every frame, scan all replicated variables, compare each to that connection's last-acknowledged state, and package deltas. Correct and simple; the per-frame per-connection scan is precisely the cost that stops scaling.

implementation_variants.name: Push-model / newer replication backend (Unreal Iris)
implementation_variants.description: Move from polling every replicated property every frame to a state where changes are pushed into the replication system, so the cost scales with what actually changed rather than with what could have changed. Epic ships Iris as a second backend alongside the legacy path, with a documented migration step.

network_relevancy_priority.applicability_conditions: Only pays for itself above a threshold of (replicated actors x connections). Below roughly a few hundred actors per connection, plain per-actor relevancy with a distance check is cheaper to build and to debug. Requires a server-authoritative replicated-state model; it is meaningless for pure lockstep (see deterministic_lockstep) where state is not replicated at all. In Unreal, this requires a source build and a C++ project, and the Replication Graph is explicitly disabled on console builds because it does not work in splitscreen.
network_relevancy_priority.limitations: The lists are only as good as the game knowledge encoded in them: a grid cell or dormancy rule that is wrong produces actors that pop in late or never update, which is a correctness bug, not a perf bug. Persisted cross-frame data must be invalidated when actors move between cells or change role. Epic's caveat that Replication Graph does not currently work in splitscreen means the console path may need a separate solution. Hand-rolled relevancy also tends to fight lag compensation, because a target you rewound to hit must still have been relevant enough to have a state history.
network_relevancy_priority.required_data_and_tools: A server CPU profiler that can attribute time inside the replication pass specifically (Unreal Insights with net/replication counters, or a hand-rolled timer around the replication-prepare phase). Synthetic load tests at target player and actor counts - a 10-player test will never expose this cost. A way to count replicated actors and per-connection bytes/second in a live match.

impact.cpu: high positive on the server - this is a server-CPU technique; Epic's stated goal is 'as few CPU cycles as possible per Actor, per client'
impact.ram: medium increase - persistent per-connection and per-cell lists are cached across frames instead of recomputed, which is exactly the trade
impact.network: slight reduction - fewer accidental 'just in case' updates; the dominant effect is CPU, not bandwidth

network_relevancy_priority.quality_impact: Neutral to positive if done correctly (Epic's explicit claim is that it solves the CPU problem 'without sacrificing the client experience'). Strongly negative if a relevancy rule is wrong: missing or late actor updates read as cheating.
network_relevancy_priority.concept_impact: Determines the maximum player count and actor density the design can support. A battle royale with loot on the ground, a 64-player shooter with persistent projectiles, and an 8-player arena are three different budget problems.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d instrument replication cost at target scale + 6d grid/room + dormancy + always-relevant nodes + 4d role-specific custom nodes + 2d load test and regression harness; using an engine-provided replication graph. A fully custom relevancy system is roughly double this.

relations.note: Relevancy decides WHICH actors are considered; delta compression decides HOW MUCH of each is sent. Both are needed and neither substitutes for the other.
The relevancy pass runs on the authoritative server; a listen-server topology changes who pays the cost and who gets the latency advantage.
Relevancy cost is paid per tick, so raising tick rate multiplies it. Riot's 2.34 ms/frame server budget leaves essentially no room for an O(actors x clients) scan.
Lockstep avoids replication entirely by sending only commands, which sidesteps relevancy - at the cost of an input delay and strict determinism.
Rewinding requires retained history for the rewound entity; if relevancy culled or never sent that entity's state, the rewind silently degrades.

network_relevancy_priority.verification: Run a synthetic load test at the real target actor and player count and measure server CPU time inside the replication-prepare phase alone, before and after. Then verify correctness, not just speed: for a set of scripted scenarios (teammate out of sight, ability-revealed enemy, loot picked up behind a wall), assert that the expected client received the update within one update interval. Finally, confirm on the console path whether the chosen solution is even active, given Epic's documented splitscreen limitation.

client_prediction_reconciliation.problem: In a server-authoritative model, if the client waits for the server before showing the result of its own input, every action is delayed by a full round trip. Valve states the problem concretely: with 150 ms latency the player would see their own forward movement 150 ms late. The fix is to let the client run the same simulation code the server runs for its own inputs, show the predicted result immediately, and then correct when the authoritative result arrives. The hard part is not the prediction, it is the correction: the server's reply describes a state from one RTT in the past, so you cannot simply snap the player to it. You must buffer inputs, rewind to the last server-authoritative state, and replay the buffered inputs forward to the present. Overwatch's formulation is explicit - prediction covers movement, abilities (weapons included) and hit registration, and reconciliation replays all cached input from the last server-authorized moment until it catches up to now.

implementation_variants.name: Input buffer + full replay on mispredict (Source / Gambetta)
implementation_variants.description: Sample input into user commands at the server tick rate, send them continuously, run them locally, and on a prediction error rewind to the server state and replay every unacknowledged command. Valve exposes cl_predict, cl_showerror and cl_smoothtime to control it and to smooth the residual error.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed command frame + ring buffer + time dilation (Overwatch)
implementation_variants.description: Quantize time into fixed command frames, run every predicting system in a fixed update (UpdateFixed, never Update), store movement in a ring buffer for comparison, and slightly dilate the client's frame time under jitter so its input stream runs ahead of the server, filling the server's input buffer against packet loss.

implementation_variants.name: Decoupled simulation with server-side input prediction fallback (VALORANT)
implementation_variants.description: Simulate movement/physics at a fixed 128 Hz independent of render framerate, queue client moves at tick granularity, and when a client update has not arrived in time have the server predict (usually 'continue holding the last keys') rather than stall. Corrections are isolated to the affected player.

implementation_variants.name: Sliding-window redundant input (Overwatch over UDP)
implementation_variants.description: The client keeps a sliding window of all inputs since the last server acknowledgement and packs the whole window into each outgoing packet. Compressed, this is cheap because players do not meaningfully change input 60 times a second, and it fills server-side buffer holes after a lost packet without a resend round trip.

implementation_variants.name: Per-ghost opt-in prediction (Unity Netcode for Entities)
implementation_variants.description: Unity's DOTS netcode is a server-authoritative + client-prediction framework where prediction is opted into per client and per ghost, marked with a PredictedGhost component, so non-critical entities never pay prediction cost.

client_prediction_reconciliation.applicability_conditions: Requires a server-authoritative model and shared simulation code between client and server - which in practice means the gameplay simulation must be separable from rendering and runnable at a fixed timestep. Requires that the predicted entity is affected only by the local player (Valve: prediction 'is only possible for the local player and entities affected only by them'). Not applicable to systems whose outcome the client is not allowed to know (e.g. hidden information, or damage numbers the client must not compute).
client_prediction_reconciliation.limitations: Prediction errors are visible as a snap or a slide if not smoothed, and misprediction cascades: Overwatch notes that at 150 ms, a movement misprediction also mispredicts the hit. Above a threshold prediction stops helping and Blizzard disables it (220 ms). Predicted projectiles can visibly vanish when the server disagrees - Blizzard accepted this as the right trade for Pharah rockets. Valve caps extrapolation at 0.25 s of packet loss because error grows too large beyond that. Every predicted system must be replayable, which forbids using non-deterministic local state inside the prediction path.
client_prediction_reconciliation.required_data_and_tools: A way to inject artificial latency and packet loss on a real build (Valve's net_fakelag equivalent), a prediction-error visualiser (cl_showerror / server-vs-client hitbox draw), and an input recorder so a mispredict can be reproduced deterministically. Deterministic replay infrastructure (see Overwatch's replay/rewind pipeline) pays for itself here.

impact.cpu: medium - the client re-simulates buffered inputs on every mispredict, and the server may predict missing client input; cost scales with the number of predicted entities and the replay window
impact.gpu: none directly, but perceived smoothness improves because the rendered state is not a round trip behind
impact.ram: low-medium - ring buffers of input and movement state per predicted entity (Overwatch keeps half a second of movement snapshots for bounding volumes)
impact.network: slight increase - redundant input windows and higher command rates cost upstream bytes; this is usually a good trade

client_prediction_reconciliation.quality_impact: Very large and direct: this is the difference between 'responsive' and 'swimming in syrup'. Riot ties correctness of prediction to 'near-perfect hit registration' and says nailing it is 'critical for making gunplay feel crisp and rewarding'.
client_prediction_reconciliation.concept_impact: Determines which mechanics can exist at all. Fast projectiles, counter-strafing, instant abilities and any twitch mechanic are only viable with prediction; a design built entirely on slow, telegraphed actions can ship without it.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 8d fixed-timestep refactor so simulation is decoupled from render + 7d input buffering, replay and smoothing + 5d server-side prediction for missing input + 5d latency/packet-loss test rig and repro tooling. Halve it if the engine already ships prediction (Unity Netcode for Entities, or UE CharacterMovementComponent).

relations.note: Prediction handles the local player; rewind handles remote players. Valve treats them as the two halves of latency compensation, and Overwatch implements both from the same buffered MovementState.
Both attack input-timing quantisation: sub-tick at the registration end, prediction at the display end. Neither removes the other's cost.
Lockstep removes misprediction entirely by never predicting - everyone waits. Overwatch explicitly declined full RTS-style determinism and relies on server correction instead.
The replay window is measured in command frames, so the tick rate directly sets how many frames of input must be stored and re-simulated.
Prediction means the client runs authoritative simulation code and knows more than it should; Riot's answer is server authority over the outcome, never trusting the client's view of the world.

client_prediction_reconciliation.verification: Run at injected latencies of 0/50/150/300 ms and at 1-5% packet loss. Assert three things: (1) the local player's position one RTT after an input matches the server's, within an epsilon; (2) a forced mispredict (e.g. server-side stun) produces a correct catch-up rather than a teleport; (3) above your declared cutoff, prediction is actually off and the client waits. Log prediction-error magnitude distribution over a soak test - a long tail means a non-determinism bug in the prediction path, not a network problem.

delta_compression_state.problem: Sending a full world snapshot to every client on every tick is linear in world size, not in what actually changed, and it is the single biggest bandwidth lever in a replicated-state architecture. The problem delta compression solves is: send only what changed since the last update the client acknowledged, and keep enough shared history on both sides that 'what changed' is well defined even when packets are lost. Valve's description is the canonical statement: the server does not send a full snapshot each time, it sends only the changes since the last acknowledged update; a full snapshot is sent at game start or after heavy packet loss. The hard engineering part is not the diff - it is the acknowledgement and baseline bookkeeping that makes a diff reconstructable, plus the CPU cost of producing diffs for every connection every tick.

implementation_variants.name: Delta against last-acknowledged baseline (Source, Quake3 lineage)
implementation_variants.description: Each packet carries acknowledge numbers; the server keeps per-client state and sends only fields that changed relative to the baseline the client acked. Quake3's sv_snapshot.c is the reference implementation of building a client snapshot by diffing entity state against the client's last acknowledged baseline.

implementation_variants.name: Per-connection dirty-variable scan and packaging
implementation_variants.description: Scan every replicated variable each frame, compare against each connection's last known state, and package the deltas. This is the mainstream engine implementation and also the one Riot identified as a CPU cost worth escaping via RPCs.

implementation_variants.name: Full-snapshot recovery path
implementation_variants.description: Keep a reliable route back to a complete state: send a full snapshot on join and after sustained loss, and let the client force one (cl_fullupdate). Without this, a lost baseline silently corrupts every subsequent delta.

implementation_variants.name: Redundant-input window instead of state deltas (command-level compression)
implementation_variants.description: For input, do not delta state at all: send a sliding window of all inputs since the last ack. Because players change input far less often than the frame rate, this compresses well and removes the need for resends.

implementation_variants.name: Backend-level delta/push modernisation (Unreal Iris)
implementation_variants.description: Replace per-frame polling of every replicated property with a newer replication backend whose cost scales with what changed rather than with what could have changed; Epic documents a migration path.

delta_compression_state.applicability_conditions: Requires a replicated-state (not lockstep) architecture and per-connection acknowledged baselines. Requires that the server can retain, per connection, the state it last knows the client to have - which is a memory and bookkeeping cost that grows with player count. Meaningless for lockstep and mostly irrelevant for games that are already well under their bandwidth cap.
delta_compression_state.limitations: The baseline is the fragility: if the server and client disagree about the baseline, every subsequent delta is garbage, which is why a full-snapshot recovery path is mandatory. Deltas cost CPU per connection per tick, so bandwidth saved is paid for in server CPU - the same trade Riot hit. Deltas also leak information less predictably than full snapshots, so a delta encoder must be written so that a malformed client ack cannot cause unbounded work.
delta_compression_state.required_data_and_tools: Per-connection bytes-per-second instrumentation (Valve's net_graph shows last incoming packet size, average bandwidth and packets per second - the exact tool for this), a packet capture (Wireshark) to verify what actually went on the wire, and a synthetic test that runs at the target player count while forcing loss to exercise the full-snapshot path.

impact.cpu: medium-high on the server - delta production is per connection per tick and is a known bottleneck in the mainstream engines
impact.ram: medium - per-connection baseline state must be retained
impact.network: high reduction - this is the primary bandwidth lever; without it bandwidth scales with world size

delta_compression_state.quality_impact: Indirect but real: bandwidth saved is bandwidth available for higher update rates or more relevant actors, both of which are directly perceived. A broken baseline produces persistent visual corruption, which is catastrophic.
delta_compression_state.concept_impact: Sets the practical ceiling on world complexity and player count for a given bandwidth budget. Also determines whether you can afford to run at a higher tick rate at all.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d baseline/ack bookkeeping + 6d delta encode/decode + 4d full-snapshot recovery and loss-path testing + 4d bandwidth instrumentation and soak. If your engine already ships delta compression (UE, Unity Netcode, Source), this collapses to ~4d of tuning and measurement.

relations.note: Relevancy shrinks the candidate set; delta compression shrinks the payload. Doing only one leaves most of the win on the table.
Delta cost is per tick; doubling tick rate doubles delta production work even if bandwidth per packet halves.
Lockstep compresses by sending commands instead of state - the extreme end of the same idea - and trades input delay for it.
The delta baseline state lives on the authoritative server, so server memory and CPU planning are part of this decision.
Both depend on the same acknowledgement bookkeeping; input windows and state deltas share an ack stream.

delta_compression_state.verification: Measure average and p99 bytes per second per connection at the target player count, then force 1%, 5% and 20% loss and confirm that (a) bandwidth does not collapse to full-snapshot rates and (b) state never desynchronises permanently. Explicitly test the 'heavy loss for a couple of seconds' path that Valve says triggers a full snapshot, and verify the client recovers. Diff the decoded client state against the server state every tick in a debug build.

headless_dedicated_server.problem: A listen server - one player's machine acting as the authority - has three defects: the host plays in the true game state and therefore has an unfair advantage, the host's own framerate and network affect everyone, and the build carries the whole client (renderer, audio, input, UI) that a server does not need. Epic's definition of the alternative is precise: a dedicated server 'runs headlessly', meaning no clients play directly in its instance, it does not render any visuals, and nobody plays locally. The engineering problem is not 'how do I run a server' - it is that a headless build is a distinct build target with its own cook, its own content, its own stripped subsystems and its own cost model per concurrent instance, and that model is what determines whether the game is economically viable at all. Riot's numbers make the economics explicit: at 3 games per core on 36-core hosts, each physical server must run 108 games / 1080 players.

implementation_variants.name: Engine server build target with separate cook (Unreal)
implementation_variants.description: Add a <Project>Server.Target.cs, build the Development Server configuration, and cook content for the WindowsServer platform separately from the client. Requires a source build of the engine and a C++ project.

implementation_variants.name: Dedicated Server platform with a scripting define (Unity)
implementation_variants.description: Build for the Dedicated Server platform; Unity defines UNITY_SERVER so server-only code can be compiled in, and the same can be driven from the command line with -standaloneBuildSubtarget Server.

implementation_variants.name: Density-optimised server hosting (Riot's model)
implementation_variants.description: Treat the server as a datacenter workload: target a fixed number of games per core, derive a per-frame ms budget from the tick rate, and tune hardware (NUMA binding, C-states, clocksource, scheduler migration cost) and code (animation every 4th frame) to hit it.

implementation_variants.name: Relayed transport instead of exposed IPs (Steam Datagram Relay)
implementation_variants.description: Carry game traffic over Valve's backbone rather than publishing dedicated-server addresses, which removes direct-IP DDoS as an operational threat and changes the deployment topology.

implementation_variants.name: Third-party anti-cheat server module on the dedicated server (EOS/EAC)
implementation_variants.description: Run the anti-cheat server interface inside the headless server: register each client at session start, carry opaque anti-cheat messages over your own networking, and handle action-required callbacks such as kicking unprotected clients.

headless_dedicated_server.applicability_conditions: Required for competitive or large-scale multiplayer where host advantage is unacceptable - Epic says dedicated servers 'are ideal for large-scale or competitive games' while a listen server 'is often acceptable for casual multiplayer and cooperative gaming'. Requires either a source build (Unreal) or the Dedicated Server platform (Unity). Requires a deployment story: host provisioning, scaling, and (strongly recommended) a transport that does not expose server IPs.
headless_dedicated_server.limitations: Cost scales with concurrent instances, and instance density is bounded by the per-frame budget - Riot's whole article is the story of getting a 50 ms server frame down to sub-2 ms so that 128 tick could be given away for free. Unreal's dedicated server path requires a source build and a C++ project, which is a real barrier for Blueprint-only teams. Headless builds still need cooked content, and forgetting this produces the documented 'missing shaders' failure on first run. Anti-cheat integration adds a hard dependency: if anti-cheat messages are delayed or truncated by your own network prioritisation, clients get kicked with HeartbeatTimeout.
headless_dedicated_server.required_data_and_tools: A headless-capable CI that can build and cook the server target, a way to run N server instances on one host for density testing, per-instance CPU/frame-time telemetry, and a load test at production concurrency (Riot found different behaviour at 1 instance vs 168 instances - 1.5 ms vs 5.7 ms).

impact.cpu: high - the server is the CPU product; a headless build removes render/audio/presentation cost but adds per-instance simulation cost
impact.gpu: none - a headless server should not require a GPU; if it does, that is a bug
impact.ram: high in aggregate - RAM per instance times instances per host is usually the density limit
impact.disk: medium - separate cooked server content; smaller than the client but not free
impact.network: high - upstream bandwidth scales with players x tick rate x payload

headless_dedicated_server.quality_impact: Removes host advantage entirely, which is a competitive-integrity quality win. Also decouples server framerate from any player's machine, so simulation consistency improves.
headless_dedicated_server.concept_impact: Enables persistent worlds, competitive integrity, server-side authority for anti-cheat, and matchmaking rather than peer hosting. Constrains the design through the per-instance cost: Riot only offered 128 tick for free because they got to 3 games per core.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 4d server build target + cook pipeline + 3d stripping client-only subsystems (render/audio/UI) + 5d density/frame-time telemetry on a multi-instance host + 3d deployment/provisioning. Excludes anti-cheat integration (see runtime_security_budget) and excludes lobby/matchmaking.

relations.note: Server tick rate and instance density are the same equation: Riot derives a 2.34 ms frame budget from 128 tick and 3 games per core.
The dedicated server is where the authoritative anti-cheat and server-authoritative validation live; EAC requires a server interface and per-client registration.
Relevancy cost is paid on the dedicated server, so server CPU density决定了 relevancy is worth engineering.
Lockstep peer-to-peer removes the dedicated server cost entirely - which is exactly why RTS games chose it - at the price of input delay and no host authority.
A headless server running hundreds of instances makes any per-frame allocation or GC pause visible as a hitch multiplied across every game on the host.

headless_dedicated_server.verification: Build and cook the server target from a clean CI machine and run it with no display attached. Then run a density test: N instances on one host while measuring per-instance frame time, and confirm the tick budget is met at the p99, not just the mean (Riot's 1 instance = 1.5 ms vs 168 instances = 5.7 ms is exactly this test). Verify the server has zero GPU and audio device dependencies. Finally verify a client can connect from a different machine on the configured port.

deterministic_lockstep.problem: Replicating the state of thousands of units costs bandwidth proportional to unit count, which on 1990s-2000s hardware was not merely expensive but impossible. Paul Bettner's Age of Empires paper quantifies the wall: passing X and Y coordinates, status, action, facing and damage per unit would have limited the game to 250 moving units at most on a 28.8 modem. Lockstep's answer is to not send state at all. Run the identical deterministic simulation on every machine, send only the commands, and schedule those commands far enough in the future that every peer has them before the turn executes. The cost is command latency; the benefit is that bandwidth becomes a function of player input rate rather than world size, and determinism becomes a free anti-cheat. The engineering burden moves entirely into determinism discipline and into making the fixed delay feel acceptable.

implementation_variants.name: Simultaneous simulation with scheduled commands (Age of Empires)
implementation_variants.description: Run the exact same simulation on every machine; tag each command to execute two communications turns in the future (commands issued in turn 1000 execute in turn 1002), so there is always a full turn of slack for delivery.

implementation_variants.name: Speed control to absorb latency variance
implementation_variants.description: Each client reports the framerate it can sustain and its longest average ping using 2 bytes per turn; the designated host computes a target frame rate and turn length each turn. Turn length rises fast to handle latency spikes and settles back slowly, adjusting only a few ms per turn.

implementation_variants.name: Out-of-sync detection as integrity enforcement
implementation_variants.description: Because every machine must produce byte-identical simulation, any divergence is detected and tagged 'out of sync', stopping the game. This made cheating 'extremely difficult' - a security property that falls out of the transport choice rather than being bolted on.

implementation_variants.name: Partial determinism with server correction (Overwatch's rejection of full lockstep)
implementation_variants.description: Keep a synchronised clock, fixed update period and quantisation for prediction quality, but do NOT require full RTS determinism: let the authoritative server correct any client that diverges. Blizzard states explicitly that they did not implement complete RTS-style determinism.

implementation_variants.name: Deterministic replay as a debugging and feature substrate
implementation_variants.description: Because the simulation is deterministic and a recording is synchronous in the same way multiplayer is, a game recording is a guaranteed-reproducible bug repro - and it is the same infrastructure that powers kill cams and highlights.

deterministic_lockstep.applicability_conditions: Best for games with high unit counts and low input rates, where players tolerate command delay: RTS, turn-based, some fighting games with rollback. Requires genuinely deterministic simulation across all target hardware - floating point, iteration order, RNG, container ordering and anything depending on local time or settings must all be pinned. Not applicable to twitch shooters: the scheduled delay is a design-level input lag that prediction-based client/server avoids.
deterministic_lockstep.limitations: Latency is paid as input delay, and the worst machine sets the pace for everyone - a slow peer degrades all peers. Every divergence is fatal: the game stops rather than repairing. Adding a player late, or allowing reconnection, is awkward. Determinism discipline is a permanent tax on the whole codebase ('programmers had to be aware that the code must not depend on any local factor'). Bettner's hidden-problems section exists precisely because these costs are subtle and only appear at scale.
deterministic_lockstep.required_data_and_tools: A determinism test harness that runs the same command stream on multiple machines and hash-compares the full world state every turn, an out-of-sync detector with enough logging to localise the first divergent field, and a latency-injection rig able to reproduce the 20-1000 ms swings the design claims to tolerate.

impact.cpu: medium - every peer runs the full simulation for every player, so CPU scales with world size on every machine rather than on one server
impact.ram: low - no per-connection replicated state; only command queues and turn history
impact.disk: very low - a match recording is a command log, which is why replays are tiny
impact.network: very large reduction - bandwidth scales with command rate, not world size; the paper's example is 250 moving units vs hundreds/thousands

deterministic_lockstep.quality_impact: Positive for world scale (thousands of units are free), negative for responsiveness: the perceived quality is entirely determined by how well speed control hides the scheduled delay.
deterministic_lockstep.concept_impact: Enables massive-unit-count designs and near-free replay/kill-cam/highlight features, and makes client-side cheating structurally hard. Forbids designs needing instant response to input.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 12d determinism audit and pinning (float model, RNG, ordering, containers) + 10d turn scheduler and command queueing + 8d speed control + 6d out-of-sync detection and divergence-localisation tooling + 4d soak/latency testing. Retrofitting determinism into an existing non-deterministic engine is easily 3x this.

relations.note: Lockstep and delta compression are two answers to the same bandwidth problem; lockstep wins when state is huge and command rate is tiny.
Prediction buys responsiveness by allowing divergence and repairing it; lockstep forbids divergence and pays in delay. Blizzard chose prediction and explicitly rejected full RTS determinism.
Relevancy exists because replication cannot afford to send everything; lockstep removes replication so relevancy has no meaning.
Lockstep is peer-to-peer and needs no game server, which is a large infrastructure cost saving and a large authority loss.
Out-of-sync detection is anti-cheat for free, but it replaces detection-and-ban with stop-the-game, which is a different product decision.
A 'turn' is a tick with an explicit delivery deadline; the budgeting problem is the same but the cost of missing the budget is a stall rather than a hitch.

deterministic_lockstep.verification: Run the same recorded command stream on every supported hardware/OS configuration and assert a byte-identical state hash at every turn - this is the primary test and must run in CI. Separately, inject latency across the documented range (20-1000 ms) and verify the game stays playable and never desyncs; specifically test alternating 80/500 ms, which the paper reports felt worse than a constant 500 ms. Verify that a deliberately desynced client is detected and reported with a localisable divergence.

tickrate_budgeting.problem: Server tick rate is the single number that couples responsiveness, CPU cost and hosting economics: it sets the quantisation of input, the per-second cost of every per-tick system (simulation, relevancy, delta production, anti-cheat bookkeeping), and therefore how many game instances fit on a host. The budgeting problem is to pick a tick rate and then fit the whole server frame - not just the simulation - inside 1/tickrate, with headroom, at production instance density. Riot's article is the only place I found where the arithmetic is published end to end: 128 tick means 7.8125 ms per frame, they wanted better than 3 games per core, and after reserving 10% for OS/scheduling overhead their target budget was 2.34 ms per frame. Valve publishes the other half of the picture: their default is a 15 ms timestep (66.666 ticks/s) and they explicitly warn that running at tickrate 100 generates about 1.5x the CPU load of the default 66, and that they do not suggest running higher than 66.

implementation_variants.name: Derive the budget from tick rate and target density (Riot)
implementation_variants.description: Start from 1/tickrate, divide by the target games per core, subtract a host overhead reserve, and treat the result as a hard per-frame budget. Then optimise code and hardware against that number rather than against 'feel'.

implementation_variants.name: Conservative engine default and an explicit warning (Valve/Source)
implementation_variants.description: Ship the engine default (15 ms / 66.666 tick/s) and document that raising it is not recommended and costs load super-linearly (~1.5x CPU at tickrate 100).

implementation_variants.name: Decouple simulation tick from render framerate
implementation_variants.description: Run movement/physics at a fixed simulation rate regardless of render rate; clients at 60 FPS simulate multiple movement ticks per frame and high-refresh clients blend one update across frames. Prevents drift between clients with different framerates.

implementation_variants.name: Per-system rate reduction
implementation_variants.description: Not every system needs the tick rate. Riot animated every 4th frame, cutting animation cost by 75% and reducing animation system cost over a round by another 33% - buying tick-rate headroom where it mattered.

implementation_variants.name: Host and OS tuning as part of the budget
implementation_variants.description: NUMA binding (50% -> 97-99% local memory, ~5%), scheduler migration cost (4%), C-state limiting (1-3% more games), clocksource choice (1-3%), and hyperthreading policy are all part of hitting a ms-level budget at density.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed command frame with a loop accumulator (Overwatch)
implementation_variants.description: Quantize time into fixed command frames and advance frame numbers with an accumulator; predicting systems run on the fixed command frame, never on the render frame.

tickrate_budgeting.applicability_conditions: Only meaningful with a server-authoritative architecture and a real hosting cost model. The right tick rate is a function of genre (twitch tactical shooters justify 128; co-op PvE rarely does), of player count, and of how much per-tick work your server does. Requires the ability to measure server frame time at production instance density - a single-instance measurement is worthless, as Riot's 1.5 ms vs 5.7 ms shows.
tickrate_budgeting.limitations: Raising tick rate raises CPU near-linearly and often worse (Valve's 1.5x at 100 vs 66), and can force you to lower player counts or raise hosting spend. It does not fix the dominant latency term: Riot's own peeker's-advantage budget shows tick rate is one of several contributors alongside RTT, client buffering and render rate. Two of Riot's hardware findings contradict each other across time (hyperthreading off helped early at 25->20 ms; hyperthreading on later gave +25%), so hardware tuning results are not portable even between revisions of the same game.
tickrate_budgeting.required_data_and_tools: Per-instance server frame-time telemetry with p99, not just mean; a multi-instance load harness on production-spec hosts; CPU profiler on the server build; and a controlled latency/buffering rig to separate tick-rate effects from RTT effects.

impact.cpu: high and direct - tick rate is the multiplier on every per-tick system on the server
impact.gpu: none on the server; on the client, higher render framerate reduces perceived latency independently of tick rate (Riot's 144 FPS result)
impact.ram: low-medium - more ticks can mean larger buffered input/state windows
impact.network: high - bandwidth scales linearly with tick rate for a fixed payload

tickrate_budgeting.quality_impact: Directly affects perceived responsiveness and hit registration. Riot's most useful published result here is a sensitivity figure: skilled players in blind playtests could identify ~10 ms changes to peeker's advantage, and 20 ms 'felt very impactful'.
tickrate_budgeting.concept_impact: Bounds the design: a game whose mechanics need sub-10 ms precision must either pay for high tick rate or adopt sub-tick input registration. It also directly sets the hosting bill, which is a business-design constraint.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3d frame-time instrumentation on the server build + 3d multi-instance load harness + 4d per-system profiling and rate reduction + 2d host/OS tuning. This assumes the tick rate is already fixed-step; changing a variable-timestep engine to fixed-step is a separate, much larger task.

relations.note: Sub-tick attacks the same input-quantisation error without raising tick rate - Valve's stated claim is that tick rate stops mattering for input registration.
The budget is a per-instance hosting budget; density and tick rate are one decision.
Relevancy and delta work are per-tick, so a tick-rate increase multiplies them.
Prediction hides the tick rate from the local player, which is why moderate tick rates are acceptable in games with good prediction.
Rewind hides the tick rate from the shooter; the amount of history you must retain scales with tick rate (Valve: 1 second).

tickrate_budgeting.verification: Instrument server frame time per instance and load a host to production density; assert p99 frame time is inside the derived budget with the OS reserve included. Then A/B the tick rate with real players and measure the outcome metric that matters (Riot used peeker's-advantage and blind playtest win rates), not just frame time. Verify no system silently runs faster than intended under load, and re-run the density test after every substantive gameplay change.

subtick_networking.problem: In a fixed-tick server, an input that happens between ticks is not registered until the next tick, so input registration is quantised by 1/tickrate - up to ~15.6 ms of error at 64 Hz. The visible symptom in a shooter is that a shot fired between ticks is evaluated against a world state from a slightly different instant than the one the player was looking at. Sub-tick networking attacks this at the source: instead of raising the tick rate (which multiplies CPU cost), timestamp the input precisely at the moment it happens and have the server evaluate that action at the reported instant rather than at the next tick boundary. The part that must be stated honestly: Valve's only verified public statement about sub-tick is a product claim on the official Counter-Strike 2 page - 'Tick rate no longer matters for moving, shooting, or throwing... servers know the exact instant that motion starts, a shot is fired, or a 'nade is thrown.' Valve has not published the wire format, the clock source, or any measurement of the improvement, so nearly everything written about the mechanism is community inference.

implementation_variants.name: Client timestamp + server evaluation at the reported instant (Valve's documented claim)
implementation_variants.description: The client records the exact instant of the input; the server knows that instant and evaluates the action there rather than at the next tick boundary. This is all Valve has publicly stated, in product language.

implementation_variants.name: Timestamped input replayed inside the tick (community model)
implementation_variants.description: The community model: the client sends input with a sub-tick timestamp each tick, and the server replays inputs at the precise reported times during tick simulation. Plausible and consistent with Valve's wording, but NOT documented by Valve.

implementation_variants.name: Priority packets for timestamped actions (community model)
implementation_variants.description: Community analysis claims CS2 sends main packets at approximately the classic tick interval plus additional priority packets containing timestamped actions shortly after. Explicitly self-described as analysis, with Valve not disclosing parameters.

implementation_variants.name: Keep the base tick rate and layer timestamps on top
implementation_variants.description: Retain an existing (documented 64 Hz for CS2) simulation tick and add timestamp ordering on top, rather than raising the tick rate. The Valve Developer Community wiki records CS2 as '64 Tickrate, with Sub-tick', hard-coded to 64.

implementation_variants.name: Server rewind to the reported instant (the mechanism sub-tick depends on)
implementation_variants.description: Any 'evaluate at the past instant' scheme requires the server to reconstruct a past world state, which is the same machinery as lag compensation. Sub-tick is not an alternative to rewind - it is a consumer of it.

subtick_networking.applicability_conditions: Worth considering only for games where sub-tick-level input precision is competitively meaningful - precise shooting, counter-strafe timing, grenade lineups. Requires that the server can reconstruct or reason about world state at arbitrary past instants, and requires a trustworthy shared clock between client and server. Requires honest handling of the fact that the timestamp comes from the client: the server must validate the reported instant against its own clock rather than accepting it.
subtick_networking.limitations: The dominant limitation is evidential, not technical: Valve publishes no spec, no measurement and no guarantee, so no performance or accuracy number can be attributed to sub-tick. Because the timestamp is client-supplied, it enlarges the client-trust surface unless bounded by the server. Community sources disagree with each other about the base tick rate (one page says Valve runs 128-tick official servers, another and the VDC wiki say 64), so even the base rate is not safely quotable from community sources. Finally, sub-tick does not remove network latency: it removes tick quantisation, which is a different and much smaller term.
subtick_networking.required_data_and_tools: A high-resolution monotonic clock shared and synchronised between client and server, a server-side validator for client-reported timestamps, and instrumentation that measures the residual difference between 'instant the client thinks it fired' and 'instant the server evaluated'. Without the last one you cannot prove the feature works at all.

impact.cpu: low-medium - timestamps add per-input data but avoid raising the tick rate; the cost is a validation and replay cost, not a simulation-rate cost
impact.ram: low - slightly larger input history to support evaluation at arbitrary instants
impact.network: low increase - timestamps add bytes per input; community analysis reports CS2 sends more data than CS:GO, but that is unverified

subtick_networking.quality_impact: Potentially high for competitive shooters (Valve's own claim is that moving and shooting become 'equally responsive' regardless of tick rate and grenades 'always land the same way'). Unverified by any published measurement.
subtick_networking.concept_impact: If it works as claimed, it decouples input precision from tick rate, which removes the main argument for expensive high-tick servers. That is a significant hosting-economics claim and should be treated as such.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 8d shared clock and timestamp plumbing + 8d server-side evaluation at an arbitrary past instant (reuses rewind machinery) + 6d anti-abuse validation of client timestamps + 8d measurement of residual registration error. Highly dependent on already having lag_compensation_rewind; without it, add ~20d.

relations.note: Two answers to input quantisation: raise the tick rate (linear CPU cost) or timestamp inputs (validation complexity). Valve's claim is that sub-tick makes tick rate stop mattering.
Evaluating an action at a past instant requires reconstructing that instant - the exact machinery of rewind, with the same abuse surface.
Sub-tick fixes when the server thinks you acted; prediction fixes what you see before the server agrees. Both are needed for a shot to feel right.
Client-supplied timestamps are a new input the server must not trust; bounding them is a security decision, not a networking detail.
No source found relating sub-tick timestamping to lockstep command scheduling, although both are about ordering inputs in time. Recorded as unknown rather than guessed.

subtick_networking.verification: Instrument the residual: for every shot, record the instant the client believes it fired, the instant the server evaluated, and whether the hit result differed from a next-tick-boundary evaluation. Report the distribution of that residual - with and without sub-tick. This is exactly the measurement Valve has not published, and without it any claim of benefit is marketing. Separately, fuzz the client timestamp (early, late, non-monotonic, absurd) and confirm the server clamps or rejects rather than honouring it.

lag_compensation_rewind.problem: Without compensation, a shooter must lead moving targets by an amount that varies with one-way latency, which Riot calls 'unintuitive for players'. By the time a shot arrives at the server, the target has moved again, so the server's world no longer matches what the shooter saw. Lag compensation solves this by having the server use the shooter's latency to rewind time when processing the user command, so the server evaluates the shot against what the player actually saw. Valve's formulation: Command Execution Time = Current Server Time - Packet Latency - Client View Interpolation; the server moves players back to that time, executes the command, detects the hit, then restores. The engineering problem is entirely in the second half: bounding how far back you are willing to rewind, deciding what entities participate, and keeping the cost and the abuse surface under control.

implementation_variants.name: Player-only rewind with a fixed 1-second history (Source)
implementation_variants.description: Keep one second of location and animation history and, by default, rewind only players. Wrap the relevant code between StartLagCompensation and FinishLagCompensation; time is wound back at the start call and forward at the finish call.

implementation_variants.name: Optimised rewind scope (Source, Alien Swarm and later)
implementation_variants.description: Choose per-invocation how much to rewind: LAG_COMPENSATE_BOUNDS rewinds locations only and skips animations; LAG_COMPENSATE_HITBOXES rewinds both (standard); LAG_COMPENSATE_HITBOXES_ALONG_RAY rewinds hitboxes only for entities actually hit by a supplied ray.

implementation_variants.name: All-entity rewind via an opt-in keyvalue (Source, L4D2+)
implementation_variants.description: Since Left 4 Dead 2 all entities can be lag compensated using the LagCompensate keyvalue, but the documentation says to 'use this sparingly' - an explicit cost warning from the engine vendor.

implementation_variants.name: Buffered MovementState + bounding-volume prefilter (Overwatch)
implementation_variants.description: Server rolls the target back to the frame the attacker reported, driven by a buffered MovementState component. Each character also carries a bounding volume that is the union of its snapshots over about half a second, which acts as a cheap prefilter. Rewind is a separate Behaviour from damage: hits on doors, platforms and the payload are rewound but produce no damage.

implementation_variants.name: Bounded rewind with an explicit abuse limit (VALORANT)
implementation_variants.description: The server rewinds to the time the client says it was looking at, but the rewind distance is capped and tuned, because otherwise a 500 ms-latency player could kill you half a second after you reached cover.

lag_compensation_rewind.applicability_conditions: Requires a server-authoritative shooter (or anything with raycast/volume hit detection against moving entities), a server-side history buffer, and a trustworthy latency estimate per client. Requires that the rewound entities' state can be restored cheaply - which means bounding which properties participate. Requires an explicit abuse policy: how far back the server will rewind, and under what conditions it refuses.
lag_compensation_rewind.limitations: Rewind is a correctness/abuse trade: the further back you allow, the more a high-latency player can kill a target that has already reached cover. Riot documents exactly this with the 500 ms example. Rewinding more entity types and rewinding animations both cost more - Valve's own doc says all-entity rewind should be used sparingly. Rewind also creates the well-known 'died behind cover' perception for the victim, and it fights relevancy: an entity that was never replicated to the shooter cannot be rewound for them. Note also that Valve's CBasePlayer does not do lag compensation by itself - a derived class must implement it.
lag_compensation_rewind.required_data_and_tools: A server visualiser for rewound vs current hitboxes (sv_showlagcompensation / sv_showimpacts), latency injection (net_fakelag) to test at realistic RTTs, and a soak test that measures server CPU inside the rewind region specifically - it runs per shot, per player, at the tick rate.

impact.cpu: medium-high - rewind runs per shot and cost scales with the number of rewound entities and whether animations are included; Valve offers cheaper modes precisely because this is a real cost
impact.ram: medium - a history buffer per entity for the rewind window (Valve: 1 second of location/animation history)
impact.network: none directly, but it changes what latency is tolerable, which affects hosting region strategy

lag_compensation_rewind.quality_impact: Large and non-negotiable for competitive shooters. Riot: 'In reasonable networking conditions, this allows for near-perfect hit registration', and nailing it 'is critical for making gunplay feel crisp and rewarding'.
lag_compensation_rewind.concept_impact: Makes hitscan weapons and precise hitboxes viable across a range of latencies. Also caps how much latency the design can tolerate: Riot's 220 ms prediction cutoff and bounded rewind together define who can play at all.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d per-entity history buffer + 6d rewind/restore around the hit path + 4d scope optimisation (bounds vs hitboxes vs along-ray) + 3d debug visualisation + 3d abuse bounding and latency testing. Subtract ~8d if the engine already ships it (Source does).

relations.note: Prediction compensates the local player's own latency; rewind compensates remote players' latency. Valve treats them as one system.
Evaluating an action at a sub-tick instant requires reconstructing that instant, which is rewind. Sub-tick is a consumer of this machinery, not a replacement.
Rewind is the classic latency-abuse surface; Riot's documented answer is a tuned bound on how far the server will rewind.
History length in seconds times tick rate is the history buffer size, so raising tick rate raises rewind memory and rewind CPU linearly.
An entity culled by relevancy has no retained state to rewind, so aggressive relevancy silently breaks hit registration at distance.

lag_compensation_rewind.verification: Play back a scripted scenario at injected latencies of 0/50/150/300 ms and assert that a shot that visually hit on the shooter's screen registers server-side, and that a shot fired after the target reached cover does NOT register beyond your declared bound. Enable the rewind visualiser and confirm the blue (rewound) hitbox matches the client's view. Then soak-test server CPU inside the rewind region and confirm it is inside budget at the maximum concurrent player count.

audio_occlusion_propagation.problem: A sound emitter behind a wall should not sound like one in the open, and a sound from around a corner should arrive as if it travelled around the corner rather than through it. Three distinct things have to be computed: (1) occlusion - is the direct path blocked, and by how much; (2) transmission - what the blocking material does to the sound that gets through; (3) propagation - how sound reaches the listener by indirect paths (reflections, diffraction around portals, pathing through openings). The engineering problem is that all three are per-source-per-frame ray/geometry queries against a scene that is too complex to test exhaustively, so the whole field is about choosing which approximation to pay for: a single raycast, N rays with M bounces, a baked probe grid, or a hand-authored room/portal graph.

implementation_variants.name: Single-raycast occlusion with a 0..1 fraction and 3-band transmission EQ (Steam Audio)
implementation_variants.description: Trace one ray from source to listener; occlusion is a fraction where 0 means fully occluded and 1 not occluded at all. Transmission is modelled as three-band EQ values applied only to the occluded portion. Cheapest option; the docs warn it can cause sudden in/out transitions and that smoother transitions cost more CPU.

implementation_variants.name: Multi-ray reflection simulation with configurable ray/bounce budgets (Steam Audio)
implementation_variants.description: Trace up to 4096 rays from the listener with up to 16 bounces, producing a 2.0-second, 1st-order Ambisonic impulse response using 2 threads. Baking can instead use 32768 rays, 1024 diffuse samples, 64 bounces and 8 threads offline.

implementation_variants.name: Probe-baked pathing for long-distance / around-corner propagation (Steam Audio)
implementation_variants.description: Generate probes on a grid (spacing 2.0 m in the documented example), bake probe-to-probe visibility with a visibility range of 50 m and a path range of 100 m, then at runtime find the shortest unoccluded probe path and render it as an Ambisonic field. Paths can be re-checked against dynamic geometry.

implementation_variants.name: Obstruction/occlusion curves driving Volume, LPF, HPF and spread (Wwise)
implementation_variants.description: Compute a scalar obstruction/occlusion value and map it through designer-authored curves onto Volume, LPF, HPF and diffraction-spread-factor. Authoring-side: an occlusion component with a Layer Mask of blocking layers, plus separate portal obstruction.

implementation_variants.name: Hand-authored Rooms and Portals with per-surface acoustics (Wwise Spatial Audio)
implementation_variants.description: Author an explicit room/portal graph in the editor and assign acoustic materials per surface, so propagation is derived from a designed space rather than from raw geometry queries. In a non-spatial-audio scene only occlusion applies; in a spatial-audio scene obstruction applies relative to the Spatial Audio listener and portals can be obstructed separately.

implementation_variants.name: DSP-graph effects with measured chain cost (FMOD)
implementation_variants.description: Insert occlusion and reverb processing as DSP units in the FMOD graph and measure them with the engine's own profiling rather than estimating; the cost is a chain cost, visible and attributable.

audio_occlusion_propagation.applicability_conditions: Requires a scene representation the audio system can query - triangle geometry, colliders, or an authored room/portal graph - plus a decision about whether dynamic occluders must be handled. Baked approaches require that the static geometry is final before baking. The choice between real-time and baked is essentially a choice about whether your levels are stable enough to bake and whether you have the disk budget for probe data.
audio_occlusion_propagation.limitations: Cheap occlusion is discontinuous: Steam Audio's single-ray mode 'may cause sudden in/out transitions', and smoothing costs CPU. Real-time reflection simulation is documented as 'very compute-intensive'. Baked approaches cannot respond to new dynamic geometry and cost disk plus a bake step in the content pipeline. Room/portal authoring is a real authoring burden that grows with level count and must be maintained. None of the vendors publish a per-source CPU or memory budget, so every cost claim here has to be measured in your own build.
audio_occlusion_propagation.required_data_and_tools: The middleware profiler (Wwise profiler / FMOD profiler) with per-voice and per-effect CPU attribution, a scene query cost counter (raycasts per frame per source), and a bake pipeline with a disk budget. For bake-based approaches you also need a re-bake trigger wired into the level build.

impact.cpu: medium-high and highly variable - from one raycast per source to 4096 rays with 16 bounces on N threads; this is the widest cost range of any method in this pack
impact.gpu: none (unless a GPU ray-tracing backend such as Radeon Rays is enabled, which Steam Audio supports)
impact.ram: medium - baked probe batches and reflection data must be resident or streamed
impact.vram: none typically; GPU-accelerated ray tracing would add a small BLAS
impact.network: none - audio propagation is a local simulation; in multiplayer it must be computed per client, which is a client CPU decision

audio_occlusion_propagation.quality_impact: High for immersion and, in competitive games, for fairness: Crytek treats Hunt: Showdown's audio as a core competitive mechanic worth a dedicated developer post. Steam Audio's case for convolution/path reverb is that it produces 'compelling environments that sound more realistic'.
audio_occlusion_propagation.concept_impact: Enables stealth and information-based design (you can hear but not see), which is a whole genre. Also creates an accessibility obligation: if audio carries competitive information, players with hearing differences need a visual equivalent.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d scene integration (geometry or colliders into the audio system) + 6d occlusion/transmission tuning with a sound designer + 6d propagation strategy (real-time vs bake vs rooms/portals) + 3d profiler instrumentation + 3d bake pipeline if baking. Authoring rooms/portals across an entire game is content work and is NOT included here.

relations.note: Reverb is the tail of propagation; both are computed from the same reflection simulation and both share the ray/bounce budget.
Propagation adds per-source DSP cost, which competes with decoding cost for the same audio thread / CPU budget.
Per-source audio simulation state allocated per frame in a managed engine produces GC pressure exactly where a hitch is most audible.

Epic's relevancy guidance mentions actors that 'can potentially be seen or heard', implying audio should feed relevancy, but I found no source documenting how to wire audio relevance to network relevance. Recorded as unknown.

audio_occlusion_propagation.verification: Measure raycasts per frame and audio-thread CPU per source in the middleware profiler, at the maximum expected simultaneous source count - not with one source playing. Verify occlusion transitions are smooth by panning a source behind an edge at varying speeds and listening for clicks. If baking, verify the bake pipeline re-runs on level change and measure the resulting disk size. Confirm that a source the player can hear but not see actually produces a usable cue at competitive distances.

audio_streaming_compression.problem: Audio competes for three budgets at once: disk/package size, resident memory, and decode CPU on the audio thread. The decision is per-asset and per-platform: which codec, at what quality and sample rate, and whether the asset is decompressed on load, held compressed in memory, or streamed from disk. It interacts with everything else in the audio budget because codec choice sets decode cost, and decode cost shares the audio thread with occlusion and reverb DSP. The honest framing: this is the audio area where vendor documentation gives you the most knobs and the fewest numbers - codecs, quality sliders and sample-rate overrides are all exposed, but no vendor I checked publishes a per-asset decode cost table.

implementation_variants.name: Per-ShareSet conversion settings (Wwise)
implementation_variants.description: Codec, quality, sample rate and channel count are defined per ShareSet, so a platform or bank can carry its own conversion policy rather than a global one.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-level import transcoding with selectable codec (Unity)
implementation_variants.description: Unity transcodes imported audio to a build-target-appropriate format; PCM and ADPCM additionally allow automatic optimisation or manual adjustment of the sample rate to reduce size further.

implementation_variants.name: Streaming from disk for long assets, in-memory for short ones
implementation_variants.description: The classic split: music and long dialogue stream; short, latency-critical SFX stay resident. The failure mode to design against is a stream buffer starved by a disk hitch, which produces an audible dropout at exactly the wrong moment.

implementation_variants.name: Measure decode cost in the middleware profiler rather than estimating
implementation_variants.description: FMOD exposes its effects and processing as a DSP graph with profiling, so decode and effect cost can be attributed and measured instead of guessed from codec folklore.

implementation_variants.name: Budget the audio thread as a whole
implementation_variants.description: Treat decode + occlusion + reverb + voice management as one per-frame budget on the audio thread, because they contend for the same time and a hitch in any of them is audible.

audio_streaming_compression.applicability_conditions: Applies to any project with more audio than fits comfortably in memory, which is most of them. The codec decision is per-platform (some platforms have hardware decoders for specific codecs). Streaming requires storage with predictable throughput - an open-world game streaming audio while streaming geometry is competing for the same I/O.
audio_streaming_compression.limitations: Lossy codecs add decode CPU and can add latency on loop points; lossless costs disk and memory. Streaming introduces I/O contention and dropout risk. Sample-rate reduction is the cheapest win and the most audible one if overdone. Most importantly: none of the sources I verified publishes a per-asset or per-voice decode cost, so any CPU budget here must be measured in-engine.
audio_streaming_compression.required_data_and_tools: The middleware profiler with per-voice CPU and memory attribution, a package-size report per platform, and a stress test that plays the maximum simultaneous voice count while streaming from the target storage medium (not from an SSD if the target ships on HDD).

impact.cpu: medium - decode cost per active voice; lossy codecs cost more than PCM/ADPCM
impact.ram: high lever - this is usually the largest single audio memory decision (decompress-on-load vs compressed-in-memory vs streamed)
impact.disk: high lever - codec and quality determine package size
impact.network: none (download/patch size is affected, which is a distribution concern)

audio_streaming_compression.quality_impact: Usually small if budgets are respected; catastrophic if a codec or sample-rate choice is pushed too far, because audio artefacts are immediately perceptible to players who may not be able to name them.
audio_streaming_compression.concept_impact: Determines how much music, dialogue and ambient content the game can carry, which is a content-scope constraint, and determines install size, which is a commercial constraint.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3d codec/quality policy per platform + 3d load-type classification of the asset library + 3d profiler instrumentation and voice-count stress test + 3d package-size and streaming-I/O validation. Content re-authoring (re-recording or re-editing to fit) is not included.

relations.note: Reverb and decoding share the audio thread; adding heavy convolution reverb reduces the headroom available for decoding and vice versa.
Same audio-thread contention: per-source occlusion queries plus decode plus reverb must fit in one frame's audio budget.
Streaming decoders are a classic source of per-frame allocations in managed engines; a zero-allocation decode path is part of this budget.
A headless server should carry no audio assets or audio runtime at all - the Dedicated Server build target is where that saving is realised.

audio_streaming_compression.verification: Produce a per-platform package-size report and a resident-memory report at the worst-case moment of the game, then run a voice-count stress test on the target storage medium and confirm no dropouts. Measure audio-thread CPU with the full chain active (decode + occlusion + reverb). Verify the streamed assets recover cleanly after a forced I/O stall.

audio_convolution_reverb.problem: Algorithmic (feedback-delay-network) reverb is cheap but generic: it cannot make a corridor sound like a corridor or a cathedral like a cathedral, and it does not change correctly as the listener moves between spaces. Convolution reverb solves this by convolving the dry signal with an actual impulse response - either measured or simulated from scene geometry - so the reverb is physically derived from the space. The cost is the problem: convolution is the most expensive per-sample operation in a typical game audio graph, and its cost scales with impulse-response length and channel count. Steam Audio is unusually explicit here: it documents the IR size and channel count directly (88200 samples at 4 channels in the worked example) and states plainly that real-time reflection/reverb simulation is 'very compute-intensive', which is why baking exists.

implementation_variants.name: Simulated-IR convolution reverb (Steam Audio)
implementation_variants.description: Simulate reflections from scene geometry to produce an Ambisonic impulse response, then convolve. The documented example uses IPL_REFLECTIONEFFECTTYPE_CONVOLUTION with an IR of 88200 samples (2.0 s at 44100 Hz) at 4 channels (1st-order Ambisonics).

implementation_variants.name: Baked-IR convolution reverb
implementation_variants.description: Bake impulse responses offline with much higher settings (32768 rays, 1024 diffuse samples, 64 bounces, 8 threads) using IPL_REFLECTIONSBAKEFLAGS_BAKECONVOLUTION, and play them back at runtime.

implementation_variants.name: Listener-space reverb with source-count-independent cost
implementation_variants.description: Place the source at the listener position to model the reverb of the listener's own space. The result varies smoothly with position and its CPU cost is independent of the number of sources - turning an O(sources) cost into O(1).

implementation_variants.name: Middleware convolution DSP with profiling (FMOD)
implementation_variants.description: Use the middleware's convolution reverb DSP (FMOD_DSP_CONVOLUTION_REVERB) and measure its cost in the DSP profiler along with the rest of the chain, rather than budgeting it separately.

implementation_variants.name: Wwise Reflect-style early reflections plus a reverb tail (Wwise Spatial Audio)
implementation_variants.description: Use the Spatial Audio rooms/portals model to drive reflections and reverb from an authored acoustic space, so designer-authored rooms carry the reverb identity instead of raw geometry simulation.

audio_convolution_reverb.applicability_conditions: Worth it when the space itself is part of the experience - cathedrals, caves, corridors, binaural/horror concepts - or when you need reverb to be spatially correct rather than merely pleasant. Requires either measured/simulated IRs or the geometry to simulate them, plus an audio-thread CPU budget with real headroom. Baked approaches require stable geometry and a bake step.
audio_convolution_reverb.limitations: Cost scales with IR length and channel count, and it is the heaviest common audio effect. Long IRs (2 s is the documented example) are expensive even partitioned. Simulated real-time reverb is explicitly 'very compute-intensive'. Baked reverb cannot respond to dynamic geometry and costs disk. And no vendor publishes a per-instance CPU figure, so the only honest way to budget is to measure in the target build.
audio_convolution_reverb.required_data_and_tools: The middleware profiler with per-effect CPU attribution, an IR authoring or baking pipeline with a disk budget, and a memory model for resident IRs. If simulating, the same geometry/ray infrastructure as occlusion propagation.

impact.cpu: high for real-time simulated IRs; medium for baked IR playback; this is the single heaviest common audio effect
impact.gpu: none (unless a GPU ray-tracing backend is used for the simulation stage)
impact.ram: medium - resident impulse responses; an 88200-sample 4-channel float IR is a little over 1.4 MB before any compression

audio_convolution_reverb.quality_impact: Large when the space matters. Valve's own case for it: convolution reverb 'results in compelling environments that sound more realistic' than the alternative.
audio_convolution_reverb.concept_impact: Enables space-as-a-character design (Hellblade's acoustic concept, cave/cathedral level identity) and makes binaural horror and stealth-audio concepts viable.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 5d IR acquisition or simulation pipeline + 5d bake pipeline if baking + 4d integration into the mix and bus routing + 4d audio-thread CPU measurement and IR length/channel tuning. Excludes per-level acoustic authoring, which is content work.

Convolution competes with decoding for the same audio-thread budget; adding a long IR reduces decode headroom.
IR loading and per-frame effect state are a common source of managed allocations in engines with a GC; a hitch in the reverb path is immediately audible.
A headless server should not run any of this; excluding audio entirely from the server build is free performance.

audio_convolution_reverb.verification: Measure audio-thread CPU with the reverb active at the maximum expected source count and in the largest space, and compare against the same scene with reverb disabled to isolate its cost. Sweep IR length and Ambisonic order and record the cost curve for your target hardware - that curve is your budget. If baking, verify the bake re-runs on geometry change and measure the disk cost of the IR set.

runtime_security_budget.problem: Anti-cheat is not a feature you add at the end; it is a set of constraints on the networking, build and operations design, and each constraint has a cost. The three costs that actually show up in a budget are: (1) a runtime cost for integrity checks and for transporting anti-cheat messages; (2) an architecture cost - server authority, which forbids trusting any client-supplied state and therefore forbids whole classes of design; (3) a platform/support cost, which is the one vendors themselves keep paying down (Riot moved Vanguard to on-demand sessions, and is actively closing pre-boot motherboard security gaps). The honest finding of this research: no vendor publishes a CPU or bandwidth budget for their anti-cheat, so the runtime number must be measured, and the parts you can actually plan with are the architectural and operational requirements.

implementation_variants.name: Session-scoped anti-cheat with bootstrapper launch and integrity catalogs (EOS/EAC)
implementation_variants.description: Protection is only active during a protected multiplayer session; the game must be launched via the Anti-Cheat Bootstrapper, which fetches the current client module, and a signed catalog of file hashes is verified on access. Requires explicit BeginSession/EndSession calls and frequent platform ticking.

implementation_variants.name: Anti-cheat message transport over the game's own networking
implementation_variants.description: The SDK hands you opaque messages to deliver; you must carry them over your existing client/server transport without corruption or truncation, and must not let your own network prioritisation starve them.

implementation_variants.name: Server-authoritative design as the primary control (VALORANT)
implementation_variants.description: Riot's stated position: VALORANT uses a server-authoritative networking model specifically to limit the types of cheats possible, and the client/server protocol is designed around the rule that the server must never trust a client's view of the world.

implementation_variants.name: Determinism as structural anti-cheat (lockstep)
implementation_variants.description: In a synchronous simulation, any divergence is detected as 'out of sync' and the game stops, which made client tampering extremely difficult - security as an emergent property of the transport model.

implementation_variants.name: Kernel-level client protection with an ongoing platform cost (Vanguard)
implementation_variants.description: Riot's kernel-level client. The cost surface is documented by Riot's own change log: on-demand sessions to reduce always-on friction, and stricter pre-boot motherboard security checks for some players.

implementation_variants.name: Server-side event logging for detection (EOS/EAC)
implementation_variants.description: Register custom events at startup and log gameplay data events as they occur; the SDK batches and rate-limits them. This is where your telemetry design and your anti-cheat design meet.

runtime_security_budget.applicability_conditions: Required for any competitive or economy-bearing multiplayer title. Requires a 64-bit OS and SDK version floors; requires Windows Service Installer setup on Windows; and is explicitly unavailable for Linux ARM64 clients, Android, iOS, consoles and VMs. Requires that the game can be launched through a bootstrapper executable, which affects launchers, store builds and dev workflows.
runtime_security_budget.limitations: The runtime budget is unpublished: no vendor documents CPU or bandwidth for the client or server module, so anything you plan must be measured. The operational constraints are hard: if anti-cheat messages are slow or lost, clients are kicked (HeartbeatTimeout), and your own network prioritisation logic is a documented cause. Peer auth can take up to 60 seconds. And the platform cost is real and ongoing - Riot has shipped changes to reduce Vanguard friction and to close pre-boot security gaps, which is support and compatibility work forever.
runtime_security_budget.required_data_and_tools: A protected-session test environment with real anti-cheat credentials (not the dev bypass), telemetry on anti-cheat kick reasons (AuthenticationFailed, HeartbeatTimeout, NullClient, TemporaryCooldown), and a client CPU/frame-time measurement with and without the anti-cheat module active.

impact.ram: low-medium - resident client module plus integrity catalog
impact.disk: low-medium - module and catalog; a Windows service install on Windows
impact.network: low but with a hard reliability requirement - opaque messages must be delivered uncorrupted and untruncated, and must not be starved by your own prioritisation

runtime_security_budget.quality_impact: Indirect but decisive for competitive games: without it, match quality collapses regardless of netcode quality. The negative quality impact is user friction - which Riot explicitly worked to reduce.
runtime_security_budget.concept_impact: Constrains design directly: no client-authoritative state, no trusting client-side hit results, limited hidden information on the client. This is a design constraint from day one, not a late addition.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 5d bootstrapper/integrity-tool/launch configuration + 5d client-server session and message plumbing + 4d kick-reason telemetry and ops runbook + 3d platform compatibility matrix + 3d CPU/bandwidth A-B measurement with the module active. Excludes server-authoritative rework of existing gameplay, which can be arbitrarily large.

Client-supplied sub-tick timestamps are a new untrusted input the server must bound.
Lockstep's out-of-sync detection is anti-cheat for free, at the price of a different trust and latency model.
