managed_gc_alloc_budget.problem: In any engine with a garbage collector (or any engine whose per-frame work allocates), the budget that matters is not total memory but allocation RATE: garbage produced per frame, which determines how often collection runs and how long each pause is. This is disproportionately damaging in two of this pack's contexts. On a game server, a pause is a hitch in every match on that host, and Riot's density model (108 games per 36-core host) means one collection can stall 1080 players at once. In audio, allocations in the per-source simulation or decode path produce a hitch that is directly audible. The difficulty is that the available documentation describes the mechanisms and the knobs but publishes almost no numbers: Unity documents incremental GC and write barriers, Unreal exposes GC clustering settings, and neither publishes a per-frame allocation budget or a pause-time figure.

implementation_variants.name: Incremental (sliced) collection (Unity, default)
implementation_variants.description: Spread garbage collection across multiple frames instead of stopping for a full collection. Unity states this is the default mode, that it does not make collection faster, and that it reduces performance spikes. The cost is additional generated code (write barriers) that tracks reference writes for the collector.

implementation_variants.name: Remove managed allocation from the hot path by construction (data-oriented / ECS)
implementation_variants.description: Store networked and simulated state as unmanaged, laid-out data rather than as individually allocated objects. Unity's DOTS netcode is built on ECS, and marks predicted entities with a PredictedGhost component on data-only entities, so the replication and prediction path allocates no per-entity managed objects.

implementation_variants.name: Tune the collector's clustering behaviour (Unreal)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal exposes GC settings in Project Settings, including a minimum GC cluster size and a maximum object count not considered by GC, so large stable object graphs can be clustered and skipped rather than re-scanned every pass.

implementation_variants.name: Instrument middleware allocation with custom allocators
implementation_variants.description: Middleware that supports custom allocators (Steam Audio exposes malloc/free callbacks) lets you attribute and cap third-party allocation, which is otherwise invisible in your own allocation profiler and is exactly where audio allocations hide.

implementation_variants.name: Set and enforce an explicit per-frame allocation budget
implementation_variants.description: Treat bytes-allocated-per-frame as a hard budget with CI enforcement, measured per system (netcode, audio, gameplay), because allocation rate - not heap size - is what creates pauses. Expert practice, not a vendor-published rule.

managed_gc_alloc_budget.applicability_conditions: Applies whenever the engine or the language runtime manages memory for you. It becomes a first-class budget item when either (a) you run many game instances per host, so one pause is multiplied, or (b) you run real-time audio, where a pause is audible. It is much less critical for a single-player game with a loading screen between every scene.
managed_gc_alloc_budget.limitations: Incremental collection reduces spikes but does not reduce total collection cost - Unity says so explicitly - and it adds write barriers, so it trades throughput for smoothness. Eliminating allocation by construction (ECS) is a whole-architecture decision, not a tuning pass. Unreal's GC is a UObject mark/sweep with clustering knobs and is structurally different from a generational managed collector, so 'GC budget' means different things in the two engines and the two must not be conflated. And because no vendor publishes a budget, any target you adopt is yours, not theirs.
managed_gc_alloc_budget.required_data_and_tools: An allocation profiler that reports bytes allocated per frame per system (not just heap size), a GC-pause-time histogram captured over a soak test, and - for servers - the same instrumentation running at production instance density on one host. For audio, a custom allocator hook into the middleware so third-party allocations appear in the same report.

impact.cpu: medium - collection cost plus the ongoing write-barrier cost of incremental mode
impact.ram: high lever - allocation rate drives heap growth and headroom requirements

managed_gc_alloc_budget.quality_impact: Entirely about smoothness. Players experience GC as a stutter, and in audio as a click or dropout, neither of which shows up in average framerate.
managed_gc_alloc_budget.concept_impact: Rarely constrains design directly, but it constrains architecture: a design requiring thousands of individually-allocated simulated entities will fight the collector for the whole project.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 4d allocation instrumentation per system + 4d collector mode selection and tuning + 5d hot-path allocation elimination (pooling / struct conversion) in netcode and audio + 3d CI budget enforcement. Retrofitting a data-oriented layout onto an existing object-oriented simulation is a separate, much larger project.

relations.note: At 108 games per host, a single collection pause stalls every match on the machine simultaneously - the pause cost is multiplied by instance density.
A GC pause longer than one tick interval directly breaks the derived per-frame server budget (Riot's 2.34 ms target leaves no room for one).
Per-source occlusion simulation state is a classic per-frame allocation site, and audio hitches are immediately perceptible.
Impulse response loading and per-frame effect state are allocation sites in an audible path.
Streaming decode buffers are steady-state allocations that should be pooled once, not reallocated per buffer.

managed_gc_alloc_budget.verification: Record a GC-pause histogram (count, p99 and max) over a multi-hour soak at production entity and player counts, and separately record bytes allocated per frame per system. Assert both against budgets you set yourself, since no vendor publishes one. Critically, re-run the server measurement at production instance density on a single host, not with one instance. In audio, verify zero allocations in the per-source simulation path by instrumenting a scene at maximum simultaneous voices.

claims.statement: Unity documents incremental garbage collection as the default mode: it spreads collection over multiple frames, does not make garbage collection faster, and reduces performance spikes related to collection.
claims.locator: Page 'Garbage collection modes' (Unity 6.0 / 6000.0 manual), opening paragraphs
claims.context: URL and page title verified, but the body was behind a consent gate during this pass and the quoted sentences come from the indexed summary. Re-read before relying on it.

claims.statement: Unity documents that incremental garbage collection generates additional code, known as write barriers, to inform the collector of reference writes - i.e. the smoothness is paid for with ongoing overhead, not just at collection time.
claims.locator: Page 'Garbage collection modes', write-barrier paragraph
claims.context: Same retrieval caveat as above. The mechanism is the transferable point: incremental collection is a throughput-for-latency trade.

claims.statement: Neither Unity's GC documentation nor Unreal's GC settings page publishes a target bytes-allocated-per-frame figure or a maximum pause time, so any allocation budget must be set by the project rather than adopted from the engine.
claims.locator: Absence across the Unity 'Garbage collection modes' page and the Unreal 'Garbage Collection Settings' page
claims.context: Stated explicitly: this is the honest answer, and it is why the effort estimate includes writing the instrumentation.

claims.statement: Unreal exposes garbage collection settings in Project Settings, including a Minimum GC Cluster Size and a Maximum Object Count Not Considered By GC, i.e. clustering is the exposed lever for reducing per-pass scan cost.
claims.locator: Page 'Garbage Collection Settings in the Unreal Engine Project Settings', settings rows
claims.context: Confirmed via the indexed page contents. Important distinction: Unreal's collector is a UObject mark/sweep with clustering, structurally unlike a generational managed GC - do not apply Unity GC advice to it or vice versa.

claims.statement: Allocation rate, not heap size, is what forces collections: 1 KB of garbage per frame at 60 fps produces about 60 KB of garbage per second, which is roughly 3.5 MB per minute of continuous allocation even though peak heap may stay small.
claims.locator: Not stated in the source; derived arithmetically to show why per-frame allocation is the right unit to budget
claims.context: The inputs are illustrative round numbers chosen to make the scaling visible, NOT a measurement of any game and NOT a recommended budget. The formula is the transferable content.

claims.statement: Steam Audio supports custom memory allocators via malloc/free callbacks, which lets a project instrument and cap middleware allocation that would otherwise be invisible to the engine's own allocation profiler.
claims.locator: Section 'Initialization' -> 'Memory Allocation' (custom my_malloc/my_free callbacks; default _aligned_malloc on Windows)
claims.context: Directly actionable and, in my reading, the single most under-used allocation lever available in game audio.

claims.statement: Steam Audio's documented configurations use 2 threads for real-time reflection simulation and 8 threads for baking, so thread count is an explicit, tunable part of the middleware's runtime behaviour rather than a fixed internal detail.
claims.locator: Sections 'Reflections' -> 'Initializing a simulator for reflections' (numThreads = 2) and 'Baking' -> 'Baking reflections' (numThreads = 8)
claims.context: Include this in allocation planning: per-thread state and per-thread scratch buffers are real allocations that scale with this number.

claims.statement: Unity's Netcode for Entities is built on ECS (data-only components) and marks predicted entities with a PredictedGhost component, so the replication and prediction path deals with unmanaged entity data rather than individually allocated managed objects.
claims.locator: prediction-n4e.md: 'Unity adds the PredictedGhost component to all predicted ghosts on the client, and to all ghosts on the server.'
claims.context: The architectural fix for allocation rate: change the data layout rather than tune the collector. This is a project-defining choice, not an optimisation.

game_examples.engine: Overwatch / in-house engine (Snow engine lineage)
game_examples.fact: Blizzard adopted an Entity Component System specifically to 'curtail complexity' in a large, growing codebase, with components as pure data and systems as the only logic - the data-oriented layout that keeps per-frame simulated state out of individually allocated objects.
game_examples.locator: GDC Vault session abstract: 'Overwatch uses a cutting-edge Entity Component System (ECS) architecture... Blizzard's team leverages ECS to curtail complexity'
game_examples.non_transferable: Overwatch's engine is C++ and has no garbage collector, so ECS there is about complexity and data layout, not about GC pauses. Do not cite Overwatch as evidence that ECS solves a managed-memory problem - it solves a data-locality and complexity problem.

game_examples.game: Unity Netcode for Entities (DOTS sample stack)
game_examples.engine: Unity (ECS / DOTS)
game_examples.fact: Unity's DOTS netcode is a server-authoritative + client-prediction framework built directly on ECS, requiring Unity 2022.2.0f1 or higher, and marks predicted ghosts with a PredictedGhost component - i.e. the entire replication and prediction path operates on unmanaged entity data.
game_examples.locator: Sections '# Unity Netcode for Entities' and '## Requirements'
game_examples.non_transferable: This is an engine capability, not a shipped game, so there is no player-facing result to copy. It also does not make allocation disappear - it moves it. Gameplay code that allocates per frame inside a system will still create garbage regardless of ECS.
